title: Preface
summary: Front matter and table of contents for Ignatius Donnelly's 1882 book "Atlantis: The Antediluvian World." Covers the book's purpose and Plato's account of Atlantis, its plausibility and the sea and flora/fauna evidence, deluge legends across the Bible, Chaldeans, other nations and America, parallels between Old and New World civilizations, alphabet origins, the Bronze Age and skull deformation, Atlantis traditions in mythology (gods as Atlantean kings, Odin, pyramids and cross, sacred metals), and Atlantean colonies (Mexico, Egypt, Mississippi, Iberia, Peru, Africa, Ireland, Aryans), ending with a reconstruction of Atlantis. Includes a list of illustrations of artifacts, maps, skulls and monuments.

summary: Introduction to the book 'Atlantis: The Antediluvian World' stating its purpose: to demonstrate that Atlantis, a large island in the Atlantic opposite the Mediterranean, existed and that Plato's account is history. Claims it was the first civilized region, the origin of many nations and populations worldwide, the Garden of Eden and mythological paradises, the source of gods and heroes in various mythologies, sun-worship religion, Egyptian civilization, Bronze and iron technology, and alphabets. Also claims it was the Indo-European and Semitic origin and was destroyed by catastrophe, with survivors spreading flood legends.

title: THE PURPOSE OF THE BOOK.
summary: The text is an introduction arguing that ancient history, including the claimed civilization of Atlantis, deserves serious study. It says Genesis's opening chapters, ancient civilizations on both sides of the Atlantic, and the origins of human civilization may be clarified by such research. It notes that Pompeii, Herculaneum, and Herodotus were once dismissed as fable and later vindicated, and cites Pharaoh Necho's African circumnavigation as an example. The author promises converging evidence from many fields.

title: Chapter II.
key_items: PLATO'S HISTORY OF ATLANTIS.
summary: Introduces Plato's account of Atlantis, preserved as one of the most valuable ancient records. Covers Plato's lineage and Solon, the Athenian law-giver who visited Egypt and attempted a verse account of the Atlantic Island from Sais priests, leaving it unfinished. Describes Solon's ten-year Egyptian stay and the priest's remark about Greek lack of antiquity. Ends with Critias introducing the tale of Athens' ancient marvellous deeds, passed down through his family.

title: PLATO'S HISTORY OF ATLANTIS

nodes.title: PLATO'S HISTORY OF ATLANTIS (intro)
nodes.summary: Excerpt from Plato's Timaeus and Critias on Atlantis. Critias recounts an story Solon heard from Egyptian priests at Sais: Egyptians call Athena Neith; Greeks lack ancient knowledge; recurring catastrophes (fire, flood) wipe out civilizations; Athens of 9000 years ago was a noble, well-governed state with a social class structure, military, and wisdom. It fought and defeated an aggressive naval power from the Atlantic island of Atlantis, which later sank beneath the sea, leaving impassable mud. Names were translated into Egyptian and back. Critias invokes Mnemosyne before narrating the war.

nodes.title: FLATO'S HISTORY OF ATLANTIS.
nodes.summary: Plato's Atlantis account: the island of Atlantis is allotted to Poseidon, who fathers children by the mortal Cleito, daughter of the earth-born Evenor and Leucippe. Poseidon encircles her hill with alternating rings of sea and land, creates hot and cold springs, and produces abundant food. He fathers five twin pairs, dividing the island into ten realms. Atlas, the eldest, becomes king, and the Atlantic Ocean is named after him. Other twins receive named territories, including Gadeirus toward the Pillars of Heracles.

nodes.title: TE ANTEDILUVIAN WORl
nodes.summary: Plato's Critias account of Atlantis: Atlas's descendants rule islands and lands toward Egypt and Tyrrhenia, with great wealth, abundant mines (including orichalcum), timber, elephants, fragrant plants and fruits. They build a royal palace complex with concentric sea and land zones, canals, bridges, harbors, and walls coated in brass, tin, and orichalcum. The central temple of Poseidon has gold, silver, and ivory decoration with gold statues. Also described are hot and cold springs, baths, and cisterns.

summary: Excerpts from Plato's Timaeus and Critias on Atlantis. Critias relays Solon's tale from Egyptian priests at Sais: recurring floods and fires destroyed civilizations; ancient Athens (9000 years earlier) was a noble, well-ordered state that defeated an aggressive Atlantic naval power, after which Atlantis sank beneath the sea. Atlantis is allotted to Poseidon, who fathers five twin pairs by Cleito and divides the island into ten realms; Atlas, the eldest, rules and names the Atlantic. Descendants grow wealthy from mines (including orichalcum), timber, and fauna. They build a palace with concentric sea-and-land zones, canals, harbors, and metal-coated walls, plus a golden-adorned temple of Poseidon, springs, baths, and cisterns.

title: PLATO' ii HISTORY OF ATLANTIS.
summary: Excerpt from Plato's Critias describing Atlantis: the royal city's layout (palace, zones, harbors, temples, gardens, racecourse, guard-houses, docks with triremes, and the outer wall), the surrounding mountainous country and fertile plain, the great circular ditch and canals used for irrigation, twice-yearly harvests, and the population and military levy (60,000 lots, 10,000 chariots, 1,200 ships). It then covers the ten kings' governance under Poseidon's laws inscribed on an orichalcum column, their sacred bull-hunt oath ceremony and judgments, and the decline of the kings' virtue, which led Zeus to assemble the gods. The text ends abruptly there.

title: Chapter III.

nodes.title: THE PROBABILITIES OF PLATO'S STORY.
nodes.summary: Argues Plato's Atlantis account is plausible, comparable to descriptions of Egypt and Peru (e.g., Prescott's Cuzco temple of gold). It lacks myths, presents a reasonable immigrant-founded history, and describes a unified empire extending from Egypt to Peru. Supporting evidence includes Azores volcanic rocks and hot springs, the Poseidon-horse link, the sacred number ten in ancient traditions, the trident symbol, and the Monte da Guia landscape. Other classical and Gallic sources, Diodorus, Theopompus, and Old Testament references to islands also mention a lost Atlantic island.

nodes.title: THE riWBABlLLTIEU OF PLATO'S STORY.
nodes.summary: Excerpt from Ignatius Donnelly's Atlantis discussion: Plato's account says Atlantis was destroyed 9,000 years before Solon, and Orphic references to Lyktonia split into islands. Covers geological time claims (European caves 500,000 years, Calaveras skull), Oppert's astronomical calculations of Egyptian 1460-year and Assyrian 1805-year zodiacal/lunar cycles converging at 11,542 B.C., Chaldean 39,180-year period, Atlanteans' diverse languages, Herodotus on Hercules, and argues Plato's story deserved credence and that sudden sea swallowing of land must be examined as possible.

nodes.title: WAS SUCH A CATASTROPHE POSSIBLE?
WAS SUCH A CATASTROPHE POSSIBLE? (intro)
nodes.summary: The text argues that the sudden destruction of Atlantis, as described by Plato, is geologically plausible. It cites evidence of repeated land rises and falls (e.g., 23 changes in Pennsylvania coal measures), continents once submerged (Lemuria, Great Britain, Sicily, Sahara), sediment thickness showing a vanished eastern continent beneath the North Atlantic, Geikie's and Winchell's accounts of coastal and land-level changes, and 18th–19th century volcanic and earthquake events (Iceland 1783, Java 1822, Graham's Island 1831, Lanzarote 1730, Santorini) as parallels.

nodes.title: 38 ATLANTIS: THE ANTEDILUVIAN WOBLD.
nodes.summary: Describes the submergence of Sindree fort and village on the Indus by an 1819 earthquake (about 2000 square miles), with Sir A. Burnes's 1828 boat visit and Lyell's commentary on the ruins. It covers the violent April-July 1815 Tomboro eruption on Sumbawa (about 12,000 population, 26 survivors, ashes, and seas flooded), the 1775 Lisbon earthquake (60,000 dead, a quay swallowing people, Humboldt's wide shaking area), and Irish volcanic events. Argues Lisbon may be linked to Atlantis's buried site.

nodes.title: WAS SUCH A CATASTROPHE POSSIBLE.'
nodes.summary: The text describes a catastrophic earthquake that destroyed the village of Ballyowen in Ireland, sparing only one family, and notes that Lisbon and Ireland lie east of a central point while the West Indies lie west of it and have suffered similar quakes. It recounts the 1692 Jamaica earthquake, which opened the ground, swallowed people, and sank about a thousand acres near Port Royal into the sea. It then covers volcanic activity in the Azores, including eruptions in 1808, 1811, 1691, and 1720, and the island of Sambrina that formed and sank. It describes a north-south line of active and extinct volcanoes through the Atlantic, including Iceland, Pico, Teneriffe, Fogo, Madeira, and several South Atlantic islands of volcanic origin, and ends with an unfinished quotation from Lyell's Principles of Geology.

nodes.title: 44 ATLANTIS: THE ANTEDILVVIAX WORLD.
nodes.summary: Describes reported volcanic activity (earthquakes, troubled water, floating scoria, smoke columns) since the mid-1700s in the mid-Atlantic near the equator, suggesting a new island may form between St. Helena and Ascension. Notes a Porto Praya (St. Jago, Azores) basalt sheet over shelly strata as precedent for Atlantic land formation. Argues Atlantis's destruction by fire and cataclysm is plausible, linking this to Verne's Captain Nemo imagery, and says Atlantis's destruction details parallel Flood legends.

Contends it is not impossible that the island was destroyed suddenly by an earthquake in a single dreadful night and day. Section is Chapter V of a text on Atlantis and the antediluvian world, with page 45-46 headers.

nodes.title: THE TESTIMONY OF THE SEA.
nodes.summary: Describes a hypothetical discovery of a sunken mid-Atlantic island near the Azores, linking it to Plato's account of Atlantis. Covers volcanic evidence (peaks, lava strata, debris), Plato's quoted description of an earthquake-driven sinking and mud left behind, and deep-sea soundings by the Dolphin, Gazelle, Hydra, Porcupine, and Challenger revealing an underwater elevation from the British Isles to South America, with a map of Atlantis and its connecting ridges.

nodes.title: THE TESTIMONY OF THE SEA.
THE TESTIMONY OF THE SEA. (intro)
nodes.summary: Excerpt from Ignatius Donnelly's Atlantis: The Antediluvian World on the Testimony of the Sea. Describes a submerged mid-Atlantic ridge (Azores, St. Paul's Rocks, Ascension, Tristan d'Acunha as surface peaks) claimed to be remains of Atlantis, citing Gardner's Eocene land theory and Gettysburg sounding discoveries near Madeira and Portugal. Discusses how ridges blocked tropical water, causing the Glacial Period and Gulf Stream formation, and notes ongoing coastal subsidence and uplift. Mentions Challenger volcanic deposits and fauna similarities between Brazil and Europe.

nodes.title: the testimony of the flora and fauna.
nodes.summary: The text argues that flora and fauna show uninterrupted land connection between Europe and America after the Glacial Period, since many genera and species are shared. It lists post-glacial animals (mammoth, woolly rhinoceros, Irish elk, musk-ox, reindeer, glutton, lemming) found on both continents. It also states that Nebraska Bad Lands fossils, identified by Professor Marsh, show the horse originated in America and evolved from a fox-sized ancestor, and asks how it reached Europe and Asia without land contact, noting it existed wild in Europe before domestication.

nodes.title: THE TESTIMONY OF THE FLORA AND FAUNA. 55
nodes.summary: The text describes evidence from fossils and domestication that ancient fauna and flora were shared across continents. Fossil camels appear in India, Africa, South America and Kansas; the cave bear matches the grizzly; the musk-ox, glutton, bison, moose, reindeer, cave lion and cave wolf match modern American species. Cattle were domesticated in Switzerland in the Stone Age, and sheep, horse, ass, hog and goat are similarly ancient. Miocene Swiss fossils show over 800 flowering species, mostly migrating to America, implying land connection, and botanist Otto Kuntze finds the same domesticated tropical plants in America and Asia, suggesting human transport.

nodes.title: THE TESTIMONY OF THE FLORA AND FAUNA. 57
nodes.summary: Discusses the banana (plantain) as a seedless plant found across tropical Asia and Africa, and argues it could not have reached America by sea or by North Pole climate, questioning Professor Kuntze's claims. Notes other American-origin plants (tobacco, maize, cocoa-nut) and the Paritium tiliaceum fiber plant. Proposes that Atlantis, a hypothesized advanced agricultural civilization, spread these plants, and considers Lemuria or land bridges as alternatives.

nodes.title: THE TESTIMONY OF THE FLORA AND FAUNA. 59
nodes.summary: Discusses the Atlantis hypothesis through flora and fauna evidence: shared plant and animal species between Europe and the Atlantic States, with few species found west of the Rocky Mountains (Asa Gray's counts of genera and species). Covers the cotton plant's American origin, its use in both Old and New World, and claims about maize, potato, and tobacco in China. Also covers the etymology of maize across languages.

nodes.title: THE TESTIMOXY OF THE FLORA AND FAUNA, 61
nodes.summary: The text discusses the origins of domesticated plants, arguing they trace to Atlantis and its colonies rather than scattered regions. It cites Darwin and Alphonse de Candolle on useful plants from Mexico, Peru, Chile, and the Old World, noting many cultivated plants have unknown wild forms. Cereals (wheat, oats, barley, rye, maize) likely were domesticated in extreme antiquity or on a vanished continent. Bentham's view that these cereals no longer exist wild is quoted. Stone Age Europe is covered: wheat and barley varieties in Swiss lake dwellings suggest southern commercial contact or colonists.

Excerpt from Donnelly's Atlantis on the testimony of the sea and of flora and fauna. Covers a submerged mid-Atlantic ridge claimed as Atlantis remains, its role in the Glacial Period and Gulf Stream, and shared post-glacial animals and fossils between Europe and America (horse, camel, cave bear). Argues domesticated plants such as banana, maize, cotton, tobacco and cereals point to Atlantis or land bridges, with pre-Columbian tobacco pipe evidence.

Supporting evidence includes Azores volcanism, the Poseidon-horse link, sacred number ten, trident symbol, and Monte da Guia. Other classical sources also mention a lost Atlantic island. title: Chapter I.
key_items: THE DESTRUCTION' OF ATLANTIS DESCRIBED IN THE DELUGE LEGENDS.
summary: The text argues that Plato's account of Atlantis's destruction is geologically plausible and that its memory survives in deluge traditions across Hebrew, Aryan, Phoenician, Greek, Cushite, and American cultures. Francois Lenormant contends the deluge tradition is universal (except among Blacks), predates racial dispersion, and is historical rather than myth, though it is imported in America and doubtful among Polynesians. Schoebel and Omalius d'Halloy, along with Quatrefages and Cuvier, dispute universality, limiting the flood to the human cradle region. Plato identifies 'the great deluge of all' with Atlantis's destruction, recounted via the priest of Sais to Solon, where Athens resisted Atlantis and was also damaged by the same catastrophe.

title: Chapter II.

nodes.title: Chapter II. (intro)
nodes.summary: Covers the Bible account of the Deluge from Genesis chapters 6 to 8. It describes humans multiplying and the sons of God taking human daughters as wives, producing giants. God limits human life to 120 years, sees widespread wickedness and violence, and resolves to destroy humanity and animals. Noah, a just man, finds grace, and he has three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

nodes.title: THE DELUGE OF THE BTBLE.
nodes.summary: Covers the Genesis flood narrative: God's instruction to Noah to build a gopher-wood ark with specified dimensions and stories, and to bring two (or seven clean) of every living kind aboard. Noah obeys, enters the ark with his family and the animals, and the rain falls forty days and nights as the fountains of the deep break open. The waters prevail 150 days, covering the mountains and destroying all flesh except Noah and those with him. God remembers Noah, sends a wind, and the waters subside and the fountains and windows of heaven are closed.

nodes.title: THE DELUOE OF THE BIBLE.
nodes.summary: Excerpt from Ignatius Donnelly's Atlantis: The Antediluvian World recounting the Genesis flood narrative: waters abate, Noah sends a raven and a dove, the dove returns with an olive leaf, the earth dries, and God commands Noah's family and animals out of the ark. Noah builds an altar and offers sacrifice, and God promises never to curse the ground again. The author then argues that Genesis and Plato agree on points including the origin of civilization in the destroyed land (Adam, Abel, Cain, Tubal-cain, Jabal, Jubal as stages of development), the great populousness and wickedness of the antediluvians, their destruction by water, and an earlier sinless golden age (Eden, Atlantis).

nodes.title: THE DELUGE OF THE BIBLE.
nodes.summary: The text argues that the Bible's Deluge account cannot be universal. Genesis's genealogy (chap. x) covers only Mediterranean-related peoples (Aryans, Cushites, Phoenicians, Hebrews, Egyptians), not Chinese, Japanese, Finns/Lapps, Australians, or American natives, who existed unrelated to Noah. Quoting Lenormant, it notes the Bible lists only the white race. Therefore the Deluge destroyed a land by water, a civilized wicked land, identified as Atlantis. It also notes the Eden location is unknown, with Church tradition pointing west beyond the ocean. Flood legends of other nations are said to support Atlantis as the antediluvian world. Intermarriage of divine 'sons of God' with 'children of men' caused the destruction, as in Plato's story; Hebrew and Phoenician links to Atlantis are noted.

summary: Genesis 6-8 Deluge account: human multiplication, sons of God and giants, God limiting life to 120 years, and resolving to destroy wicked humanity; Noah, the just man, and his sons Shem, Ham, Japheth. Covers the gopher-wood ark, animals boarded, forty days of rain, 150 days of waters, and subsidence. Donnelly's Atlantis excerpt covers the raven and dove, Noah's altar, the covenant, and parallels with Plato's golden age. Argues the flood was not universal: Genesis genealogy covers only Mediterranean peoples, so the destroyed civilized land was Atlantis, with intermarriage as the cause.

title: Chapter III.

nodes.title: THE DELUGE OF THE CHALDEANS.
THE DELUGE OF THE CHALDEANS. (intro)
nodes.summary: Chapter III of Atlantis: The Antediluvian World describes two versions of the Chaldean Deluge legend. The first is Berosus's account of King Xisuthros, warned by Cronos (Ea) to build a vessel, who survives the flood, releases birds, lands on an Armenian mountain, and is taken to the gods. The second is the Gilgamesh-era cuneiform epic of Khasisatra, told via George Smith's decipherment: the ship's construction, the gods' deliberation, the storm, the birds, the sacrifice, and Bel's anger. Lenormant's comparison to Genesis is noted. The author links Chronos/Saturn to the Atlantic 'Saturnian continent' and Atlantis, and notes Ea as a fish-god.

nodes.title: THE DELUGE OF THE CHALDEANH.
nodes.summary: Excerpt from Ignatius Donnelly's Atlantis, Chapter III on the Chaldean Deluge legend. Argues Bel/Baal was an Atlantean-linked sea god and that the Chaldean flood story, unlike Genesis, describes a sea-side cataclysm: a seven-day storm with thunder, earthquakes, and a ship-like ark, versus Genesis's inland forty-day rain and chest-like ark. Notes Izdhubar's fifteen-day sea voyage to Khasisatra as hinting at Atlantis.

Covers two Chaldean Deluge legends from Atlantis (Donnelly). First, Berosus's account of Xisuthros, warned by Cronos/Ea to build a vessel, who survives, releases birds, lands on an Armenian mountain, and is taken to the gods. Second, the Khasisatra epic (Gilgamesh era, via George Smith): ship building, divine deliberation, storm, birds, sacrifice, Bel's anger. Compares to Genesis, links Chronos/Saturn to the Atlantic Saturnian continent and Atlantis, and notes Bel as a sea god, the seven-day sea-side storm versus Genesis's forty-day inland rain, and Izdhubar's fifteen-day voyage.

nodes.title: THE DELUGE LEGENDS OF OTHER NATIONS.
nodes.summary: Describes the Deluge legends of other nations, focusing on the Syrian/Aramean tradition from the Hierapolis (Bambyce) sanctuary. It recounts Deucalion's flood story: a wicked earlier race destroyed by water, Deucalion saved in a coffer with animals, and a chasm at Hierapolis that swallows floodwaters, commemorated by twice-yearly seawater pouring rites. Lenormant links this to Koran references to a bubbling oven, and compares Berosus's Xisuthros with Deucalion and Noah.

nodes.summary: The text covers Hindoo, Chaldean, Iranian and Greek deluge legends. The Brahmana tells of Manu rescued by a fish that he tows to the Mountain of the North; the Puranas name Satyravata and add the seven-day warning and the sacred scriptures saved from Hayagriva. Yima's garden refuge, guarded by the bird Karshipta, is Iranian. Greek accounts include Ogyges, Deucalion's coffer on Parnassus with the Hydrophoria rite, and Megaros. The author reads these as pointing to Atlantis, its empire, Poseidon as fish-god, and bronze-working people.

nodes.title: THE DELUOE LEGENDS OF OTHER NATIONS.
THE DELUOE LEGENDS OF OTHER NATIONS. (intro)
nodes.summary: Covers flood legends across cultures linked to Atlantis: Greek heroes who survived (Cerambos, Perirrhoos, Merops of Cos, Telchines/Sasion of Crete, Saon of Samothrace); Panathenaea festivals commemorating a war with the Atlanteans; Proclus on Atlantic islands dedicated to deities; Persian, Koranic (oven/waters) and Welsh triad Deluge accounts (Dwyfan and Dwyfach, Noah-like vessel); Norse Ymir/Bergelmir and Edda prophecy of cataclysm; and the claim that Egypt lacks any Flood allusion.

nodes.title: normant says
nodes.summary: The text argues that Egyptian records omit a universal Deluge because they preserved the history of Atlantis's local destruction, which later inspired Flood legends. It cites Manetho's claim that Thoth inscribed knowledge on stelae before a cataclysm, and notes Egyptians said Greek flood myths were local catastrophes. It then describes Cosmas's 6th-century Christian world map, where the earth is a body surrounded by water, with a transmarine land beyond it where Eden and early humans were located, and Noah's ark carried men to the inhabited world.

nodes.title: TEE DELUGE LEGE.VJJS OF OTHER NATIOXS.
nodes.summary: Discusses Cosmos's traditions placing the Deluge in the west, with Noah traveling from there to the Mediterranean shores, and recognizes western land beyond the ocean as a possible echo of Atlantean times. Includes a illustration description of a northern mountain behind which the sun sets, causing day and night alternation, with the moon looking on; the mountain is compared to the crooked Culhuacan of Aztec tradition. Notes Paradise is located in the east.

Flood legends linked to Atlantis across cultures: Greek survivor heroes, Panathenaea commemorating a war with Atlanteans, Proclus on dedicated Atlantic islands, Persian, Koranic, Welsh and Norse Deluge accounts, and the claim Egypt has no Flood allusion. Argues Egyptian records preserved local Atlantean destruction that inspired Flood myths, citing Manetho's Thoth stelae. Describes Cosmas's 6th-century world map with Eden in a transmarine land and Noah's ark, Deluge traditions placed in the west, a northern mountain causing day and night, and Paradise in the east.

nodes.title: THE DELUGE LEGENDS OF AMERICA.
nodes.summary: Describes Alfred Manry's remark that American Deluge traditions closely resemble the Bible and Chaldean accounts, while noting the Asian migration routes and Buddhism cannot explain it. The text then argues the similarities stem from knowledge of Atlantis, with America's great nations as Atlantean colonies sharing its civilization, language, religion, and blood, spanning Mexico, Yucatan, Brazil, Bolivia, Peru, and the Mississippi region.

nodes.title: THE DELUOE LEGENDS OF AMERICA.
nodes.summary: Describes American Deluge legends, mainly Mexican traditions (Coxcox/Tezpi, Xochiquetzal) with a cypress or raft refuge, a vulture and hummingbird sent out, and a landing on Colhuacan. Covers the Codex Vaticanus four-ages cosmogony, the Aztec Nahui-atl flood tale with its fish transformation, and the Nata/Nena cypress ark. Compares these to Plato's Atlantis, Genesis and the Chaldean account, arguing the resemblances are not accidental or missionary interpolations.

nodes.title: ATLANTA: THE ANTEDILUVIAN WORLD.
nodes.summary: Excerpt from Ignatius Donnelly's Atlantis: The Antediluvian World on flood legends. It compares the Aztec hero Nata/Noah name root, the Popul Vuh Central American flood account (Hurakan, storm, darkness, collapsing houses and caves) with the Chaldean legend, and traces the word hurakan to Old World storm words. It cites the Toltec flood account from Ixtlilxochitl (fifteen cubits, a tower refuge, seven Toltec wanderers), matching Genesis depth. It also covers Aztec and Chibcha (Bochica, Chibchacum) legends and the Aztlan starting point, all read as Atlantis echoes.

nodes.title: ATLANTIIS: THE ANTEDILUVIAN WOULD.
key_items: THE DELUGE LEGEXDti OF AMERICA.
nodes.summary: The text covers the Nahuatlacas and Aztecs, whose origin is linked to Aztlan, which is equated with Atlantis as a 'Eastern' homeland that dominated Central American colonies and gave them civilization. It cites the Popul Vuh's account of Quiche princes sailing east to receive royalty, and Valentini's description of a Mexican flood picture with Coxcox and Xochiquetzal on the Calendar Stone. Indian flood legends from the Great Lakes, Canada, Mississippi, and Chippewa traditions are summarized, including the ark-like raft, animals losing speech, and a fallen 'Great Spirit' father. Rafinesque's Lenni-Lenape songs describe a golden age, a snake-priest's corruption, a deluge, Nana-Bush, migration, and a frozen sea. The Mandan 'Big Canoe' ark image and its ceremonies are described, with notes on the Mandans' white ancestry and pottery skills.

nodes.title: ATLANTIS: THE ANTEDILUVIAX WOELD.
nodes.summary: Describes a ceremony in which a dignified, white-painted man named Nu-mohk-muck-a-nah ("the first or only man") arrives at a village and is welcomed by chiefs. He tours each lodge, recounting a catastrophic flood and claiming he alone survived in a big canoe. Each household gives an edged tool, which is later sacrificed by throwing it into the river. The text also mentions four sacred water-filled tortoise-shaped sacks in the medicine lodge, said to hold waters from the four quarters of the world.

nodes.title: THE DF.LUGE LEGENDS OF AMERICA.
nodes.summary: Catlin, unaware of Atlantis theory, declines to advance claims against a 'ridiculous belief.' He describes a water-sack he could not buy, and a twelve-man dance around an ark, with painted participants representing the four cardinal points and races, horned headdresses evoking Baal, and a 'Bel-lohck-na-pie' name. The author reads this as evidence of Atlantis's destruction in a flood: an ark, a messenger reporting the flood, a sacrifice, and a tortoise symbolizing an island. The text also cites a poem about St. Thomas, and the four rivers of Atlantis, and says the Mandans were of the same race.

nodes.title: ATLANTIC: THE ANTEDILUVIAN WOliLI).
nodes.summary: Covers the Lewis and Clarke account of a Native American origin legend in which the whole nation lived in an underground village beside a subterranean lake, climbed a grapevine to reach the surface, and was cut off when a heavy woman broke the vine. The text interprets this as memory of an underground settlement beyond the sea and of colonies on the American continent, cut off by a misfortune. It also cites Iowa and Dakota legends of ancestors crossing water from an eastern island in skin canoes, and Dakota tales of huge skiffs floating for weeks, as reminiscences of ancient sea voyages.

nodes.title: THE DELUOE LEGENDS OF AMEHIVA.
nodes.summary: Discusses Mandan flood legend of a world-tortoise, dove and willow, and white miners whose digging pierced the shell, linked to Atlantis; compares Mandan words with Welsh and Dakota words with Old World languages. Surveys flood legends across Iroquois, Chickasaw, Sioux, Okanagan (Scomalt, lost island), Nicaraguan, Apache (Montezuma and coyote), and Pima (Szeu-kha surviving on resin ball) traditions, concluding that these echo the sudden destruction of Atlantis.

nodes.title: SOME CONSIDERATION OF THE DELUGE LBGENDS
nodes.summary: Discusses Atlantis as possibly having volcanoes, since its ridge contains the Azores, Canaries and other volcanic features, and the sea floor along its axis is still volcanically active. Cites eruptions that projected hot water and mud: Java's Galunggung, a 1831 Sicily island with a 60-foot water-spout, and Dominica in 1880. Dominica's convulsions, which like Atlantis had hot springs, are described via a New York Herald account of a storm, sulphur smell, flooding, and volcanic debris containing iron pyrites.

nodes.title: SOME CONSIDERATION OF THE DELUGE LEGENDS. 121
SOME CONSIDERATION OF THE DELUGE LEGENDS. 121 (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes a passage on the Dominica Boiling Lake and a mud/water deluge: mud shower over Roseau and southeast areas, sulphur odor, fish killed in Pointe Mulatre River, springs running white, and volcanic activity continuing. It compares this to other deluge legends (Welsh Llyn-llion, Irish Mangerton and Slieve-donart lakes, Chaldean and Aramaean flood accounts) and argues Atlantis's destruction may similarly have involved a volcanic water outpour.

nodes.title: SOME CONSIDERATION OF THE DELUGE LEGENDS. 123
nodes.summary: Discusses Deluge legends across cultures and their links to Plato's Atlantis account. Covers the Genesis reference to the fountains of the great deep, the Chaldean water-spout and Aramaean volcanic-water traditions, and the Hindoo flood-god Hayagriva. Describes the Azores as the surviving remnant of Atlantis's lofty mountains, with Hindoo and Chaldean mountain-refuge motifs. Addresses Plato's mud-blocked navigation, paralleled in Chaldean, Popol Vuh, and Dominica accounts, and volcanic debris evidence from Challenger, Pompeii, Iceland (1783), and Sumbawa (1815).

nodes.title: SOME CONSIDERATION OF THE DELUGE LEGENDS. 125
nodes.summary: The text discusses parallels among Deluge legends. It describes Atlantis's ships returning to find the sea blocked by volcanic ash and pumice, and the resulting loss of contact with the Western continent. It notes that Phoenician, Egyptian (Thoth/Manetho), Hebrew (Seth/Josephus), and Chaldean (Ea/Khasisatra, Berosus/Xisuthros) traditions all describe knowledge being recorded on stelae, columns, or tablets before the flood to preserve it, and later recovered or translated.

Covers a Dominica Boiling Lake mud/water deluge (mud shower over Roseau, sulphur odor, fish killed, white springs, ongoing volcanic activity) and compares it to deluge legends: Welsh Llyn-llion, Irish Mangerton and Slieve-donart lakes, Chaldean and Aramaean floods, and the Hindoo flood-god Hayagriva. Argues Atlantis's destruction may have involved volcanic water outpour; the Azores as Atlantis's mountain remnant; Genesis fountains of the great deep; Plato's mud-blocked navigation paralleled in Chaldean, Popol Vuh, and Dominica accounts; volcanic debris from Challenger, Pompeii, Iceland (1783), Sumbawa (1815). Atlantis ships find the sea blocked by ash and pumice, cutting contact with the Western continent. Phoenician, Egyptian, Hebrew, and Chaldean traditions record knowledge on stelae or tablets before the flood, to be recovered later.

nodes.title: ATLANTIC: THE ANTEDILUVIAN WOULD.
key_items: SOME CONSIDERAriON OF THE DELUGE LEGENDS. 127
nodes.summary: Excerpt from Ignatius Donnelly's Atlantis: The Antediluvian World comparing flood legends. Covers the Hindoo Bhagavata-Purana fish-god warning of a flood and Plato's Critias account of Atlantean laws inscribed on orichalcum columns at Poseidon's temple. Describes Central American books and Challenger expedition evidence of a continent destroyed by three or more convulsions, with festivals commemorating them, parallels in Welsh triads, Celtic traditions, and Greek Ogygian and Deucalion deluges. Argues Atlanteans lived in perpetual terror, explaining primeval religion, pillar-inscribed records, and the Tower of Babel legend, implying an antediluvian alphabet and writing shared across both continents.

summary: Chapter III surveys deluge legends as evidence for Atlantis. It covers Chaldean accounts (Berosus's Xisuthros, the Khasisatra epic) and legends of Syria, India, Iran, Greece, Egypt, and Cosmas's map. American traditions get extended treatment: Mexican, Central American (Popol Vuh, Toltec, Aztec, Chibcha), and North American tribal stories (Mandan, Lenape, Iowa, Dakota, Lewis and Clark, Catlin, Iroquois, Pima). Volcanic eruptions at Dominica and elsewhere, plus volcanic debris, are linked to Atlantis's destruction. The chapter closes with Plato's Critias and Donnelly's view of inscribed Atlantean records and a shared antediluvian writing.

title: Chapter I.

nodes.title: Chapter I. (intro)
nodes.summary: The text argues that material civilization, defined as humanity's inventions and discoveries for controlling nature, was largely inherited from Atlantis. It describes savage life as hunger- and fear-driven, then traces key advances: the bow and arrow, fire and cooking, pottery, metallurgy, and iron-working. Such progress took thousands of years. Phoenicia, Egypt, Chaldea, India, Greece, and Rome transmitted arts without major improvement for six thousand years. Modern steam and electricity are new additions. Herodotus and Egyptian records show Egypt was already advanced at its start, with monotheism, medicine, and mature art. Scholars including Winchell, Owen, Renan, and Taine support the idea of long prior development in an original homeland. Civilization is not spontaneously reinvented or universally achievable, and the gap between civilized and savage peoples is vast.

nodes.title: ATLANTIS: TRi: ANTEDILUVIAN WOULD.
nodes.summary: Excerpt from Ignatius Donnelly's Atlantis discussing the gap between savagery and civilization, arguing no savage people has advanced independently. It cites Gauls, Goths, and Britons as possessing written languages, religion, iron weapons, agriculture, walled towns, wheeled vehicles, and a grain-cutting machine. It contends Roman and Gallic civilization differed only in degree, both drawn from a common Atlantean source. It argues that similar arts and customs across the Atlantic imply shared origin, not independent invention, since independent invention of identical technologies is improbable.

summary: Chapter I argues that material civilization (inventions for controlling nature, such as the bow, fire, pottery, metallurgy, and iron) was largely inherited from Atlantis, not reinvented independently. It notes savage life is hunger- and fear-driven, that progress took millennia, and that Egypt was already advanced at its start. Donnelly's excerpt cites Gauls, Goths, and Britons as civilized peoples, claims Roman and Gallic civilization differ only in degree, and argues shared arts across the Atlantic imply a common origin.

title: Chapter II.

nodes.title: Chapter II. (intro)
nodes.summary: Covers architecture shared by Atlantis (per Plato), Egypt, Europe, and the Americas: walls receding inward, narrow tops on doors, obelisks paralleled by Central American round columns, and a phallus-worship origin. Also covers mound-building across Europe, Asia, and America, including Herodotus's Scythian king burial, Homer's Achilles and Hector mounds, and Alexander's mound, with Foster noting resemblance to Mound Builder rites.

nodes.title: CIVILIZATIONS OF THE OLD WORLD AND THE NEW. 139
nodes.summary: Covers ancient mound and pyramid monuments: Hephaestion's and Semiramis's large mounds, and pyramids in Egypt, Assyria, Phoenicia with parallels in Mexico and Central America. Describes stone grave-cists in American mounds matching British kistvaen, and Yorkshire tumuli with wooden coffins like Mississippi Valley mounds. Notes burial goods (arms, trinkets, food, clothes, funeral urns) are shared across both continents.

nodes.title: ATLASTLS: THE ANTEDILUVIAN WOULD.
nodes.summary: Compares ancient Atlantean and Old/New World civilizations, arguing shared traits across continents. Covers construction (cement, arches, brickmaking, ornamentation), metallurgy (copper, bronze, gold, silver, iron), sculpture, painting, engraving, agriculture (plowing rituals), public works (roads, aqueducts, bridges, postal systems), navigation, manufactures, music, weapons, and religion (sun worship, embalming, priesthoods, vestal virgins, divination). Also discusses flood and cataclysm myths, ghost beliefs, animal superstitions, shapeshifting, and mythological parallels such as Pan, Atlas, Deucalion, and Medusa.

nodes.title: ATLANTliS: THE ANTEDILUVIAN WORLD.
nodes.summary: The text, from Ignatius Donnelly's Atlantis: The Antediluvian World, argues that Old World and New World civilizations share striking parallels. It covers American Indian and European idols and oracles, petrification myths, witchcraft (wax figures), and folklore links between Southern U.S. Black communities and South American tribes. Shared customs include fermented drinks, toasts, marriage and divorce, triumphal processions, bonfires, circumcision, bards, agricultural fairs, censuses, land redistribution, sacred fire renewal, and caste systems. Astronomical and calendar parallels include planet worship, the 365-day year with intercalary days, Mexican and Asian sixty-year cycles, and the eclipse-dragon myth. Other links are cremation, the Couvade custom, funerary practices, food offerings to the dead, clan-based marriage restrictions, and widow sacrifice.

nodes.title: ATLANTIC: THE ANTEDILUVIAN WORLD.
ATLANTIC: THE ANTEDILUVIAN WORLD. (intro)
nodes.summary: Covers comparisons between ancient Old World and New World (American) cultures: poisoned arrows, bark and skin canoes, rafts, stone-boiling, animal mask dances (Mandan, Tibet, Yule mummers, Dionysia), tattooing and its totemic survivals, war paint, temples built over graves, Etruscan and fairy folklore (Ojibbeway, Otoe, Shoshone), tree worship, baptism and cake offerings, floating reed islands, and marriage customs including bride-carrying and the bride-cake.

nodes.title: CIVILIZATIONS OF THE OLD WORLD AND THE NEW. 159
nodes.summary: Covers Mexican and Peruvian marriage rites (priest blessing, mantle tying, painted skeleton shawl), the organized priesthood's roles (education, marriage, confession, festivals, celibate convents, strict discipline), king's ascension rite as high priest, and cloistered monks. Also notes Mexican priests' punishment for dishonesty and incense use, first fruits supporting priests, Isthmus priests' celibacy, and American phlebotomy as a superstition later continued in Europe. Ends with Max Muller's claim of shared Indo-European folk-lore origins and links between American and other fairy tales.

nodes.title: CIVILIZATIONS OF THE OLD WORLD AND THE NEW. 161
CIVILIZATIONS OF THE OLD WORLD AND THE NEW. 161 (intro)
nodes.summary: The text compares folklore across cultures. It describes a Central American story where brothers plant canes to signal their life or death, paralleled by a Grimm tale of golden lilies and Hindoo stories, which Max Muller notes as remarkable. It then compares an Ojibbeway tale and an Irish tale, both about birds racing to fly highest: the eagle carries a hidden linnet or wren that rides on its back and wins, with the eagle keeping honor and the wren confined to hawthorn bushes.

nodes.title: THE AMERICAN STORY.
nodes.summary: The text covers Hindoo and Aryan/Turanian folk tales in which a mortal man marries a being of aerial or aquatic origin on the condition that he never breaks a rule, and the bond ends when he does. Examples include Urvasi and the rams, Raymond of Toulouse and Melusina, and Wampee and the star maiden who escapes in a basket. It also mentions Cadmus and Europa, a North American tale of a daughter carried off by the king of the buffaloes, and the spread of shared games from India to Lake Superior.

nodes.title: CIVILIZATIONS OF THE OLD WOULD AND THE NEW. 163
nodes.summary: Text from Ignatius Donnelly's Atlantis (ante-diluvian world) discusses cross-cultural parallels between the Old World and New World. Covers shared games (pachisi/patolli, ball game matching European chueca/hockey), and shared customs: baptism-like rites, prayer, sun/moon/star worship, confession, priesthood, marriage by joining hands, weapons, couvade-like husband bed rest, tattooing, intoxicating drinks, dress, cooking, metals, exorcisms, bleeding, belief in ghosts, music, dances, mummification and seated burial, mounds, pyramids, temples. Argues these similarities imply contact via Atlantis, which Plato describes as common source of arts, sciences, architecture, sculpture, navigation, writing, agriculture, roads and canals.

Compares folklore across cultures: a Central American brothers-and-canes story and a Grimm golden-lily tale (Max Muller notes Hindoo parallels); Ojibbeway and Irish bird-race tales where a hidden wren rides the eagle to win. Covers Hindoo, Aryan and Turanian tales of mortal men bound to aerial or aquatic wives under a taboo (Urvasi, Melusina, Wampee, Cadmus and Europa, a North American buffalo-king tale), and shared games from India to Lake Superior. Donnelly's Atlantis argues Old and New World parallels (games, baptism, prayer, sun worship, couvade, mummification, pyramids, mounds) imply contact via Atlantis.

Compares Old and New World cultures: poisoned arrows, canoes, rafts, stone-boiling, animal mask dances, tattooing, war paint, grave temples, folklore, tree worship, baptism, marriage customs. Covers Mexican/Peruvian marriage rites, organized priesthoods (celibacy, discipline), kingly high-priest rites, phlebotomy superstition, and Max Muller's Indo-European folklore origins. Compares tales (brothers and canes, golden lily, bird race, mortal-bound-to-aerial/aquatic-wife taboo stories) and shared games, and Donnelly's Atlantis contact argument.

summary: Chapter II argues that Atlantean, Egyptian, European, and American architecture share traits (receding walls, narrow door tops, obelisks and round columns, phallus-worship origins) and that mound-building appears across continents, including Herodotus's Scythian burial, Homer's mounds, and Alexander's mound. It compares pyramids, stone grave-cists and kistvaen, and wooden-coffin tumuli, and shared burial goods. It surveys shared arts, metallurgy, public works, navigation, music, weapons, and religion, plus flood myths, folklore, games, customs, calendars, and Donnelly's argument for Atlantean contact.

title: Chapter III.

nodes.title: AMERICAN EVIDENCES OF INTERCOURSE WITH EUROPE OR ATLANTIS.
key_items: Dr. Le Plongeon says of the columns at Chichen
nodes.summary: The text, a chapter from Ignatius Donnelly's Atlantis, presents American evidence of contact with Europe or Atlantis. It covers bearded figures in Central American monuments and the Quetzalcoatl legend of a white, bearded eastern visitor; Central American traditions of eastern origin (Tulan, Olmecs, Xicalancans); Brasseur de Bourbourg's analogy between Xibalba and Atlantis; Yucatan migration traditions and culture-hero Zamna; Mexican Aztlan legends; Bochica and Brazilian Same; elephant representations in mounds, pipes, and Palenque carvings; and Atlantis's elephants per Plato. It then covers corroborating evidence: the Meropes link, and the etymology of Atlas/Atlantic from Nahuatl atl (water).

nodes.summary: Chapters IV–VI of Ignatius Donnelly's Atlantis argue, via corroborating evidence, that a lost Atlantis existed. Points include: etymologies of 'Atlantic' and 'Atlas' from Nahuatl and Plato; Atlas mountains and Atlantes in Africa; Plato's description of the sea and America's shape; Basque language kinship with American languages; negroid and red-skinned figures in the Americas and Egypt; Mediterranean civilization radiating outward; Guanche, Egyptian, and American mummification and shared customs; ocean-origin myths; parallels between Hindu, Welsh, Phoenician, and Mayan names; diverse complexions among Europeans and Native Americans; red as a sacred color; Ptolemy's matching city names; stone-age tool parallels; and Genesis/Quiche/Mexican legends (Creation, Eden, Babel, Flood, circumcision, baptism, scalping, monotheism) suggesting a common source.

summary: Chapter III of Donnelly's Atlantis covers American evidence of contact with Europe or Atlantis: bearded figures and the Quetzalcoatl legend, eastern-origin traditions (Tulan, Olmecs, Xicalancans), Brasseur de Bourbourg's Xibalba-Atlantis analogy, Yucatan and Aztlan migration myths, Bochica, elephant depictions, and the Meropes link and Nahuatl etymology. Chapters IV-VI add corroboration: etymologies, Basque and American language ties, shared mummification and customs, Genesis-like legends, and common-source arguments.

title: Chapter VII.

nodes.title: THE ORIGIN OF OUR ALPHABET.
nodes.summary: Chapter VII of Atlantis: The Antediluvian World traces the origin of the phonetic alphabet. It notes that the European alphabet can be traced back to Egyptian, Phoenician, Hebrew, and Cushite forms, but its ultimate origin is unknown. Egyptians called hieroglyphs the language of the gods, and writing was attributed to Thoth/Taautus/Hermes. Drummond and Rawlinson suggest pre-Flood origins; Humboldt and Baldwin describe the shift from pictographs to phonetic signs. The text lists letters the Greeks and Romans added. It then examines the Maya alphabet recorded by Bishop Landa, arguing its simplified glyphs (faces, circles, serpent forms) parallel Phoenician letters like H, O, M, and N, suggesting Atlantean origin.

nodes.title: ATLAATLS: THE ANTEDILUVIAN WOULD.
nodes.summary: The text is from Ignatius Donnelly's *Atlantis: The Antediluvian World*, comparing letters of the Maya alphabet with Old World scripts. It argues that Maya glyphs for n, k, t, a, q, c, p, r, l, h, e, i, and m match forms in Egyptian, Phoenician, Ethiopian, Hebrew, Greek, Etruscan, Pelasgian, Chaldaic, and Roman writing. Donnelly traces how each sign simplified over time, citing Moab stone, Schliemann's Troy finds, and Egyptian hieratic forms, and concludes the resemblances show the Phoenician alphabet descended from Maya writing.

nodes.title: THE ORIOIN OF OUR ALPHABET.
nodes.summary: Discusses the origin of the alphabet by tracing letter forms to a Maya alphabet. Covers the Maya sign for the soft c sound (ca) and its resemblance to k and s signs across Egyptian, Phoenician, Greek, Hebrew, Samaritan, Ethiopic, Chaldaic and Illyrian scripts. Claims eighteen ancient letters trace back to Maya, with examples for h, o, t, q, k and n. Notes Maya lacks d and r, that d and t shared one sign in Phoenician and Finnish/Lapp did not distinguish them, and that Phoenicians later made d and r from the Maya b sign.

nodes.title: THE ORIGIN OF OVR ALPHABET.
nodes.summary: The text discusses the origin of the alphabet, arguing that the Maya alphabet (via Landa) resembles the Egyptian and Phoenician alphabets, with about 13 of 16 letters matching in form and sound, suggesting a common source rather than chance. It cites Phoenician legends of Taaut and Isiris, Hebrew vau and F-letter parallels, and an 1880 American Philosophical Society article on Egyptian and Maya signs (B, H, U, D). It also compares Chiapenec and Hebrew word lists and notes Maya month signs built from letters.

nodes.title: THE' ORIOm OF OUR ALPHABET.
nodes.summary: The text, from Donnelly's Atlantis, argues that Maya hieroglyphs from Copan and Palenque show the origin of the Phoenician/European alphabet, implying American-European contact and a civilization predating Europe's oldest. It cites widespread belief among ancient nations (Druids, Hindus, Hebrews, Egyptians, Chinese, Goths, Spaniards, Greeks) that writing existed before the Flood, and Plato's account of Atlantis engraving laws on bronze and gold. It also notes Josephus, Suidas, Berosus, and Mitford on antediluvian letters.

summary: Chapter VII of Donnelly's Atlantis traces the origin of the phonetic alphabet to Egyptian, Phoenician, Hebrew and Cushite forms, with ultimate origin unknown. It cites Egyptian and other traditions attributing writing to Thoth/Hermes and pre-Flood origins, and Humboldt and Baldwin on pictograph-to-phonetic shifts. It argues Maya alphabet glyphs (via Landa) match about 13 to 18 ancient letters in form and sound, suggesting Atlantean or Maya origin, noting differences in d and r. It also cites Phoenician legends, Maya Copan and Palenque hieroglyphs, Plato's Atlantis laws, and antediluvian writing references by Josephus, Berosus and others.

title: Chapter VIII.

nodes.title: THE BRONZE AGE IN EUROPE.
THE BRONZE AGE IN EUROPE. (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes the Bronze Age in Europe as the third of three ages (Stone, Bronze, Iron). Bronze (about nine parts copper, one tin) is abundant in Ireland and Scandinavia. Scholars debate its origin: no pure copper or tin age is found in Europe, while America shows a long Copper Age, especially around Lake Superior. The text rejects Roman and Phoenician authorship, citing ornamentation style, burial forms, lead content, and iron use, with reference to Lubbock, Wilde, and de Fallenberg.

nodes.title: THE BRONZE AOE IN EUROPE.
nodes.summary: Argues the Bronze Age in Europe was spread by a maritime, metalworking people rather than the Phoenicians or Etruscans alone. Cites Desor on bronze's foreign tin and copper and lead-free alloys, and the Tokhari (Celtic-type) defeated by Rhamses III. Notes Tokhari depictions on Egyptian and Assyrian monuments. Suggests the Atlantean civilization, possibly linked to copper or Atlantic trade, supplied metals. Mentions Lake Superior mining as a possible copper source and Cornish tin, with Morlot's Hallstadt evidence.

nodes.title: THE BRONZE AGE IN EUROFE.
nodes.summary: Excerpt from Ignatius Donnelly's Atlantis: The Antediluvian World on the Bronze Age in Europe. It describes ancient copper mining on Lake Superior and Isle Royale, and argues that a seafaring civilization, identified with Atlantis, spread bronze metallurgy across Europe and America. It cites Plato, Mitchell, Humboldt, Lubbock, and Wright on bronze discovery, Bronze Age domesticated animals, racial skull and hand sizes, Icelandic Irish relics, and identical bronze swords and celts across regions. It also covers Baal worship, a possible magnetic compass, house urns, lake dwellings, razor-knives with ship motifs, the word 'bronze' from Basque, and pottery, spiral designs, and vases matching American mound-builder artifacts.

nodes.title: THE BRONZE AGE IN EUROrE.
nodes.summary: Covers the Bronze Age in Europe as evidence linking it to Atlantis: double-spiral designs found in Central America, Mycenae, and Tennessee; Egyptian bronze and tin sourcing; lake-dwelling plants and jade axes of African/Egyptian origin; similar copper axes and pottery in Indiana, Ireland, Switzerland, and Mexico; eight reasons tying Europe's Bronze Age to an American Copper Age and Plato's Atlantis. Also covers artificial skull deformation among Americans, Scythians, Huns, Avars, and Crimeans.

nodes.title: ARTIFICIAL DEFORMATION OF TEE UKULL. 269
nodes.summary: Describes artificial skull deformation (flat-heads) across cultures: Swiss, French, Peruvian, Quinook, Palenque, Egyptian and Scythian examples. Cites Tylor, Wilson, Gosse, Thurman, Hippocrates, Lund, Schomburgh. Argues the practice stems from a common origin imitating a receding-forehead ancient race. Covers skull shape comparisons across races, Mound Builder and Neolithic boring of skulls, and platicnemism in leg bones.

nodes.title: ARTIFICIAL DEFORMATION OF THE SKULL. 215
nodes.summary: Argues that artificial skull deformation, found across Europe and America, is evidence of shared ancestry. The receding forehead of the Inca royal line may be natural or artificially produced. Further proofs of prehistoric racial unity include the couvade, circumcision, shared religious beliefs and customs, folk-lore, alphabetical signs, language, and flood legends. A Peruvian Inca skull from the Paucamarca cemetery is illustrated, and the page is headed Atlantis: The Antediluvian World, Part IV, The Mythologies of the Old World.

Excerpts from Donnelly's Atlantis cite shared bronze tools, Baal worship, lake dwellings, and artifacts matching American mound-builders, and link double-spiral designs, Egyptian tin, and jade axes across regions. Covers artificial skull deformation across cultures, platicnemism, couvade, circumcision, shared myths, language, and flood legends as evidence of common ancestry.

key_items: TRADITIOXS OF ATLANTIS.
summary: The text traces allusions to Atlantis in ancient traditions across many peoples. Arabian legends describe the Adites, descended from Ad (Atlantis), as a giant, sun-worshipping, architecturally advanced race with a catastrophic flood and a paradise garden (Irem). Parallels are drawn to Sabaean wealth, Peruvian sun temples, Phoenician and Egyptian religion, and the Cushite empire. Hindu Aditya gods, Persian Mashab-Ad, Chaldean Ad-mi, Genesis Adam, Cain's lineage, Guatemalan At-tit, and Mexican Atl-tona-ti-uh are linked to Ad-lantis, suggesting all these races descend from a remembered lost land.

title: Chapter II.

nodes.title: THE KINGS OF ATLANTIS BECOME THE GODS OF THE GREEKS.
THE KINGS OF ATLANTIS BECOME THE GODS OF THE GREEKS. (intro)
nodes.summary: Lord Bacon's view that Greek mythology was an echo of an older people's beliefs introduces the claim that Greek gods were deified kings of Atlantis. It surveys sun and nature worship across Peru, Egypt, Phoenicia, Babylon, India, Rome, and American tribes, and cites a Sais priest's account to Solon. It argues Greek myths, with gods who were born, died, and dwelt on Olympus, reflect human rulers, and that Atlantis is the key to Greek mythology.

nodes.title: KIXGS OF ATLANTIS THE GOBS OF THE GREEKS. 287
nodes.summary: The text, from Atlantis: The Antediluvian World, argues that Greek gods, Olympus, and the Garden of the Hesperides correspond to the lost island of Atlantis in the far west. It describes twelve principal gods on Olympus, Atlas and Chronos as Atlantean kings, and the Golden, Silver, Bronze, and Iron Ages ending in a flood (Deucalion's). It draws parallels to Plato's Atlantis account, Hesiod, Baldwin, Murray, Delaware and Mandan traditions, Babylonian and Hindu twelve-god motifs, and suggests Olympus derives from Atlantis linguistically.

nodes.summary: The text argues Greek mythology is a history of Atlantis, whose kings and empire were the basis of the Greek gods. Relics from heaven were preserved in temples, and the author rejects theories that gods were atmospheric or astronomical myths, comparing it to how names don't disprove existence. It traces Uranos, Gaea, Titans, Cyclopes, and Hekatoncheires as Atlantean peoples, linking Poseidon, Pluto, Jupiter, and Oceanus to Atlantic realms. Homer's Phaeacians, Calypso, and Odysseus's voyages are connected to Atlantis. The Cyclopes and Hekatoncheires are read as ship-related imagery, possibly gunpowder. Berosus's Oannes legend is seen as a ship tradition. Chronos's succession and the swallowing of children are also introduced.

nodes.summary: Excerpt from Scott's Atlantis (Ignatius Donnelly-style) chapter on Greek and Roman gods as remnants of Atlantis. Covers Chronos (Saturn) swallowing children, the Titan rebellion, and Saturn's rule in Italy as a Golden Age tied to Atlantean colonization. Describes the Saturnalia festivities as a memory of that age. Retells Zeus as a benevolent ruler and the Philemon and Baukis flood tale. Lists Zeus's wives and offspring, and Hera's conflicts with Zeus and Poseidon. Presents Poseidon as Atlantean first king, horse-domesticator, sea ruler, and founder of Mediterranean colonies, Athens, and Trojan links.

KlXiJS OF ATLANTIS THE GODS OF THE GREEKS. 805 (intro)
nodes.summary: Excerpt from a discussion of Atlantis and Greek mythology. It covers Poseidon/Neptune as lord of a sea palace, chariot-driver, and earthquake god, linked to Atlantis and Plato's plain. It describes how Demeter taught plough and barley cultivation at Eleusis, Dionysos spread viticulture and arts across the world, and Nymphs were female inhabitants of Atlantis's plains, related to the Atlantids. It also covers the Hesperides and their golden apples tree guarded by the serpent Ladon, slain by Hercules, and Heracles as a son of Zeus, king of Atlantis.

nodes.summary: The text argues that the Greek gods were actually kings of Atlantis, not creators of the world. Supporting points: they were human-like and fought battles; they civilized Mediterranean shores; they dwelt on an Atlantic island in the far west; their land was destroyed by a deluge; Poseidon and Atlas ruled; their empire reached Egypt, Italy and Africa; they existed in the Bronze and early Iron Ages. The Geryon cattle-raid myth is read as a memory of raids on Atlantean cattle herders. Greek mythology is thus a degenerate memory of a vast ancient empire spanning Europe, Asia, Africa and America.

Demeter taught plough and barley at Eleusis; Dionysos spread viticulture and arts. Nymphs were Atlantean plain inhabitants related to the Atlantids. Hesperides' golden apples are guarded by the serpent Ladon, slain by Hercules, a son of Zeus and king of Atlantis. Poseidon and Atlas ruled; their empire reached Egypt, Italy, Africa, and America. The Geryon cattle raid recalls raids on Atlantean herders; Greek myth is a degenerate memory of this empire.

nodes.title: THE GOD ODIN, WODEN, OR WOTAN.
THE GOD ODIN, WODEN, OR WOTAN. (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers the Scandinavian god Odin (Woden/Wotan), who resembles Zeus, dwells in Asgard, and is linked to Atlantis and Votan. It describes the Chiapanese Votan legend of migrating to America, Votan's claimed travels and ties to the Hivites, and parallels in African tunnel accounts. It then discusses the cross as a sacred symbol across ancient cultures, its association with the Garden of Eden and Atlantis, Plato's central mountain, and similar paradise myths in Greek, Scandinavian, Chinese, Singhalese, and Buddhist traditions.

nodes.title: PYRAMID, GROSS, AND GARDEN OF EDEN.
nodes.summary: The text, from a work on Atlantis, argues that the Hindu sacred mountain Meru, the Hebrew Garden of Eden, and Plato's Atlantis describe one land with four rivers flowing from a central mountain, the origin of the Cross symbol. It cites Josephus, Hindu, Scandinavian, Chinese and other traditions, and Aztec and Mixtec legends of a mountain-island paradise and deluge. It links Phoenician alphabet and Sanchoniathon's genealogy to Genesis figures like Cain and Lamech, and concludes Atlantis and Eden are the same. It finally ties pyramids across India to Peru to Atlantis's original model.

nodes.title: PYRAMID, CROSS, AND GARDEN OF EDEN
nodes.summary: Discusses the pyramid as a feature of the Atlantis problem: Arabian traditions link pyramids to the Flood, and pyramids and crosses may echo Atlantis structures and the Garden of Eden's sacred mountain. Covers the cross-on-mount symbol across cultures (Callernish, Yggdrasill, Bo-tree, crux ansata, Gnostic tombs, goddess cones), Aztlan imagery, pyramids as tombs, temples and observatories (Herodotus, Proclus), sun and fire worship in Peru, Maltese cross carvings in Mexico, Peru and Assyria, and the Bindh Madhu temple at Benares with its cross-shaped pyramidal design.

nodes.title: FYHAMIB, cm OSS, AND GAMDEN OF EDEN.
nodes.summary: Discusses pyramids worldwide as sacred structures: Hindu temples (Mathura, Elephanta, Ellora, Salsette, Chillambrum) and Babylonian/Beliis ruins; Mexican pyramids at Cholula and Teotihuacan, with size comparisons to Egypt's Cheops pyramid; Garcia y Cubas's eleven parallels between Teotihuacan and Egyptian pyramids; flat-topped and perfect-pointed American pyramids; Egyptian mastabas, Assyrian and Phoenician pyramids, and Brocard's account of Marathos.

nodes.title: PYRAMID, CROSS, AND GARDEN OF EDEN.
PYRAMID, CROSS, AND GARDEN OF EDEN. (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes Egyptian and Mexican pyramids as similar: both align to cardinal points and contain small passageways. Details the Pyramid of Teotihuacan's gallery, inclined passage, and square wells, citing Almarez and Bancroft. Compares these to the Pyramid of Cheops' passage, sepulchral chamber, and connecting passages. Ferguson is quoted arguing the resemblances are too striking to be mere coincidence.

nodes.title: FTRIMID, CROSS, AND GAIWEN OF EDEX.
nodes.summary: Covers pyramids in Egypt and America as tombs and developed mounds, with examples like Silsbury Hill in England, Irish and Ohio stone vaults, and Central American earthworks. Argues the cross and pyramid symbols on both sides of the Atlantic reflect a shared Eden or Atlantis memory of a flood-destroyed island. Then introduces money: gold and silver as sacred metals, with a table of items used as currency across cultures and the shift from utility goods to government-stamped tokens.

nodes.title: GOLD AND SILVER SACRED METALS OF ATLANTIS. 345
nodes.summary: Discusses gold and silver as sacred metals in ancient America and Atlantis. Covers Mexican tin and copper T-shaped coins, a Caribbean gold-trade anecdote, gold as sun's tears and silver as moon's color, Cuzco's Temple of Gold and its immense riches, Peruvian metal taxes and accumulation, Spanish treasure hauls, and Plato's account of Atlantean temple hoards. Argues metals were valued for sacred status, not utility, and that sun-gold commanded ten times the demand of moon-silver.

nodes.title: OOLD AND aiLVER SACRED METALS OF ATLANTIS 347
nodes.summary: Describes Atlantean sacred metals: gold and silver linked to the sun and moon. Covers the Sanskrit origin of the word karat, Assyrian consecration of gold and silver to sun and moon, and a seven-stage Nineveh pyramid with planetary colors. Notes English new-moon customs like 'turning one's silver' as relics of moon-worship. Argues modern banking perpetuates this ancient gold adoration, and that a currency limited by natural laws may harm the growing world economy more than bleeding harmed medicine.

title: Chapter I.

nodes.title: Chapter I. (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes how Atlantis's western shores lay near the West Indies, so seafaring peoples could island-hop to the mainland. Commerce between Atlantis, Yucatan, Honduras and Mexico founded trading-post colonies along the Gulf that spread inland to Mexico's highlands. Central American and Mexican traditions point to an eastern land beyond the sea, called Aztlan, remembered as a happy homeland of peaceful ancestors and origin of their civilization.

nodes.title: THE CENTRAL AMEBICAX AND MEXICAN COLOXIEH. 349
nodes.summary: Excerpt on Central American and Mexican civilization (Atlantis-themed chapter). Cites Dr. Le Plongeon claiming Maya language is partly Greek and related to Sanskrit/Assyrian. Argues Central America was once densely populated, highly advanced, possibly white-race. Desire Charnay describes vast ruins at Teotihuacan and Tula, fair bearded Toltecs, Quetzalcoatl, and antiquity evidence from broken bricks and pottery. Compares masonry, cement, sculpture, arch, bricks, glass, porcelain, bronze, coins, candlesticks with Old World; Toltec religion, farming, cotton, Cross symbol, gem-cutting, animal carvings, burial customs like Egyptian mummies. Describes Mexico's elective monarchy, social estates like Europe, and thirty grand nobles with vast vassal levies.

nodes.title: THE CENTRAL AMERICAN AND MEXICAN COLONIES. 351
nodes.summary: Describes the Central American and Mexican (Aztec) colonies' society: an estimated three million population, a feudal land-tenure system where nobles held land for military service, and an independent judiciary with life-tenured supreme, district, and local magistrates. It covers a periodic legislative assembly presided over by the king, formal marriage rites with court-supervised divorce, tolerated slavery with light labor, slaves' property and child rights, and a religion resembling Christianity (confession, absolution, baptism with holy water), as well as the numerous, powerful priesthood.

Covers women's lives and feasting customs (flowers, tobacco, turkey, chocolatl, maguey drinks). Compares Central American arch construction at Palenque with Mycenaean treasure-houses and Etruscan vaults, and notes Mexico's decline under European rule.

nodes.summary: Chapter II, 'The Egyptian Colony,' argues Egypt was a colony of Atlantis, citing: Egyptians' claimed descent from the twelve gods (Poseidon, Cleito and ten sons); Phoenician legends (Misor, Taaut/Thoth, Chronos giving Egypt to Taaut); Biblical descent from Ham; similarities to American civilization; claimed red-man origin; sun-worship and parallel sun-god names across cultures; pyramids in Egypt and America; Egypt's knowledge of Atlantis despite not being maritime; the western under-world of the dead, reached by crossing water, with its Elysian Fields and river Uranes; and Egypt's sudden, fully developed writing and skill, quoted from Blackwood. It concludes Egypt was a golden bridge from a mighty Atlantean civilization, illustrated by monuments like the Great Pyramid, Lake Moeris, the Labyrinth, and Karnak.

nodes.title: THE EGYrriAN COLOXY.

Covers its vast monuments and temples, an early society with monogamy, women's property rights, humane treatment of slaves and captives, and a moral code with forty-two commandments. Notes Egyptian advances in mathematics, astronomy, land surveying, chemistry, metallurgy, glassmaking, dentistry, music, and surgery. Compares Egyptian calendars and obelisks with Mexican and American Indian structures, and cites scholars who say Egypt appeared suddenly with no primitive origins. Concludes that Egypt's achievements and the 13,900-year 'reign of the gods' suggest Atlantean origins.

nodes.title: THE COLONIES OF THE MISSISSIPPI VALLEY.
nodes.summary: Describes a hypothesis that a maritime people planted colonies around the Gulf of Mexico and up the Mississippi River, which is consistent with the Mound Builders of the Mississippi Valley being a river people whose densest settlements lay along the Mississippi and its tributaries. Cites Foster that navigable streams were the Mound Builders' highways, and Fontaine's claim that they built levees to control bayous for agriculture and commerce. Notes there is no evidence they reached the Atlantic coast.

THE COLONIES OF THE MISSISSIPPI VALLEY, 371 (intro)

Covers their massive earthwork mounds (e.g., Cahokia, comparable in base area to Cheops), circular and square enclosures of precise geometry, and fortifications like Fort Ancient. Also covers their metalworking in copper, silver, lead, and possibly iron, including silver-plated copper bosses, casting, Lake Superior copper mining, shell beads suggesting lathe use, and comparisons to Egyptian, Mexican, and European cultures.

It cites evidence of great antiquity, cultivated plants, domesticated animals, and a Davenport tablet. It argues for links to Atlantis, Central America, Europe's Bronze Age, and the Nahuas. nodes.title: THE PERUVIAN COLONY.
nodes.summary: The text argues that Atlantis expanded westward up the Amazon into Bolivia and Peru, forming a Peruvian colony of fair-skinned, bearded founders. It describes Quichua/Inca civilization: vast ruins (Tiahuanaca, Gran-Chimu, Cuelap), aqueducts, long stone-paved roads, enormous gold and silver wealth, and Lopez's claim that Quichua is an Aryan language. It lists over twenty cultural parallels with the Old World (sun worship, embalming, vestal nuns, decimal organization, castes, knighthood, owl-headed vases, Pelasgian architecture) and concludes that these resemblances stem from common origin in Atlantis.

nodes.title: THE AFRICAN COLONIES.
THE AFRICAN COLONIES. (intro)
nodes.summary: Discusses the racial mixing in African populations, from light Berbers to very dark Lolofs. It covers traces of red or copper-colored races, Prichard's four classes of true Negroes, and Abyssinian and Nubian variation. It describes Barbary Berbers and Moors, including their physical traits, and Tuaregs. It covers Foolahs (Fulbe), who vary in color and are thought by some to be Mediterranean-type. It discusses Faidherbe's theory that dolmen (cromlech) builders in Africa and Europe were one migrating race, linked to the Tamahu and Masas peoples. It concludes that colonists from three races (white, yellow, red) may be linked to Atlantis.

nodes.title: THE IRISH COLONIES FROM ATLANTIS.
nodes.summary: Describes Irish colonization from Atlantis per the text: ancient legends of pre-Flood Spanish fishermen and Lady Banbha's settlers; the Formorians, a piratical warlike people from the West (Africa meaning 'the West'), possibly Atlanteans; Partholan's Spanish-origin people defeated; Neimhidh's invasion; Fir-Bolgs, Tuatha-de-Dananns, and Milesian Basque/Iberian invasion around 1700 BC; dating of these events; and the Fir-Bolg/Tuatha battle account with shared language.

nodes.title: THE miSH COLONIES FROM ATLANTIS.
nodes.summary: Excerpt from Ignatius Donnelly's Atlantis (ch. on Irish colonies). Covers Tuatha-de-Danann and Fir-Bolg civilization, Formorians (Balor) and their Hebrides base, and Irish legends tracing Partholan's people, Nemedians, Fir-Bolgs, Tuatha-de-Danann and Milesians to Magog's descendants and Atlantean origins. Discusses the Milesian migrations via Egypt, Crete, Scythia, Africa and Spain. Argues Celtic/Aryan migrations came from Atlantis, not Asia, citing linguistics. Argues the Deluge was local, Irish civilization is ancient, sun-worship was Ireland's original religion, Druidic practices (metempsychosis, human sacrifice) and Bel/Baal worship parallel other ancient peoples.

nodes.title: THE HUSH COLONIES FJiOM ATLANTIS.
nodes.summary: The text covers Atlantean origins of Irish culture: sun-worship fire rituals (Beltinne, St. John's-eve fires, cattle driven between fires), Irish customs paralleling Egyptian, Roman, Greek, and Hindoo practices (keening, wakes, sneezing blessings, jacks, wren reverence, pilgrimages), and the argument that these reflect common Atlantean origin rather than Hindoo migration. It cites round-towers in Ireland, Shetlands, Sardinia, and Colorado as evidence, plus Diodorus on Ireland, traditions of a western land, the Abbe Brasseur's account of Irish contact with America, and St. Brendan's seven-year voyage west c. 545. It includes a poem about Tir-na-n'oge, identified as Atlantis. Final section introduces Max Müller's claim that Aryan and Semitic languages stem from Noah's descendants.

Sections on Irish colonization from Atlantis (Formorians, Partholan, Fir-Bolgs, Tuatha-de-Danann, Milesians) and Donnelly's arguments on Celtic origins, sun-worship, Druidic practices, Irish customs, round-towers, St. Brendan's voyage, Tir-na-n'oge, and Max Müller's language claims.

nodes.title: THE OLDEST SON OF NOAH.
THE OLDEST SON OF NOAH. (intro)
nodes.summary: Excerpt from Atlantis: The Antediluvian World (Chapter VIII, 'The Oldest Son of Noah'). Quotes Max Müller on three language/religion families (Turanian, Aryan, Semitic/Hamitic) radiating from Noah and a primitive shared Semitic religion centered on El. nodes.title: THE OLDEST SON OF- NOAH.

It also cites Chinese flood legends, Sir William Jones, and M. Terrien de la Couperie's linguistic comparison of Chinese and Chaldean words.

nodes.title: THE OLDEST SON OF NOAU.
nodes.summary: Excerpt from an 1880s-style work on Atlantis (page 433-434) arguing that Aryan, Semitic, and Hamitic languages derive from a still older mother-tongue, the language of Noah and Atlantis. It gives etymological examples: Arabic, Hebrew, Chaldee, Ethiopian, and Sanskrit roots tied to English, Latin, Greek, Welsh, Norse and German words (inn, fall, fool, spear, yoke, senile, found, break, rain, reach, cover, shackle, lad, matter, meet). It concludes that all Atlantean races once shared one language, and that the Babel dispersion reflects tongues splitting over vast time.

nodes.title: THE OLDEST SOX OF NOAH.
nodes.summary: The text, from Atlantis: The Antediluvian World, argues that the Chinese and Otomi (Mexican) languages share deep resemblances, with a word list comparing Chinese, Othomi, and English terms. It cites Forchhammer on Ural-Altaic similarities with Choctaw and related languages, and suggests Chinese and Indian similarities arose through Atlantis rather than the Bering Strait. It reinterprets Genesis's Noah's sons as races: Phoenicians, Arabians, and Hebrews as Hamitic, Turanians as Japhetic, plus the Aryans. It details Turanian-American parallels in religion, sun worship, customs, calendars, quipu, hieroglyphics, and architecture across Asia and America, quoting Humboldt, Prescott, Lenormant, and Ferguson.

Section on the oldest son of Noah, tracing Atlantean and Noachic origins of world languages and religions. Covers Max Müller's three language families (Turanian, Aryan, Semitic/Hamitic) and shared El-centered religion; Semitic and Egyptian deity names linked to Atlantis; Etruscan and Ugro-Finnish origins; Central Asian and Chinese ancient history and flood legends; etymological links among Indo-European and Semitic words; Chinese, Otomi and Turanian-American parallels in religion, architecture and language; and horn and bull symbolism.

summary: Hypothesis that a maritime Atlantean people colonized the Gulf of Mexico and Mississippi Valley, where Mound Builders settled densely along river systems. Covers Cahokia earthworks, metalwork, relics, and proposed links to Atlantis, Central America, and Bronze Age Europe. Traces Iberian colonies across Europe and Britain, the Basques, and Peruvian Quichua/Inca parallels with Old World culture. Examines African racial variation and colonization, Irish settlement traditions, and Noah's-son origins of languages and religions, including Max Müller's language families and flood legends.

title: Chapter IX.

ANTIQUITY OF SOME OF OUR GREAT INVENTIOXS. 441
summary: Argues that Atlanteans invented the magnetic compass and gunpowder and that many later technologies trace back to them. Evidence includes ancient magnet lore across Phoenician, Hindu, Chinese, Egyptian and American cultures, the Hercules and cup myths, and Hannibal's alleged gunpowder use. Also covers early navigation and ship sizes, iron, paper, silk, agriculture, civil government, and astronomy. Ends with a table of inventions and their attributed inventors, concluding a lost advanced civilization preceded Egypt and Greece.

title: Chapter X.

nodes.title: THE ARYAN COLONIES FROM ATLANTIS.
THE ARYAN COLONIES FROM ATLANTIS. (intro)
nodes.summary: The text, from Atlantis: The Antediluvian World (Chapter X), argues the Aryan/Japhetic peoples originated in Atlantis. It cites Genesis's list of Japhethite nations, Winchell and Rawlinson on shared Aryan-Semitic-Hamitic origins, and Armenia (Mount Ararat) as the Aryan migration center, reachable from Atlantis by sea. It describes Iberian and Celtic links, Titans and Celts, Plato's earth-born men, and Max Müller's reconstruction of early Aryan civilization (marriage, kinship terms, towns, farming, metals, ships, decimal system). It contrasts this with the lack of wild-animal vocabulary, suggesting a sheltered, long-civilized sea-isolated homeland like Atlantis.

nodes.title: THE AHYAX COLOXIES FROM ATLANTIS.
nodes.summary: An excerpt from Ignatius Donnelly's Atlantis: The Antediluvian World arguing that Aryan and other ancient peoples descended from Atlantis. It covers Egyptian and Greek accounts of Dionysos, Amon, Chronos and Zeus; the Hindu figures Indra and Deva-Nahusha, linked to Meru and the 'Meropes' of Atlantis; Pururavas and Nahusha's legends; Rig-Veda sun-worship hymns and paradise beyond the seas; the Dolphin's Ridge; three racial groups (Shem, Ham, Japheth) and Greek Titans and Giants; and Aryan migration, the seven Aryan branches, and their European dominance.

nodes.title: THE ARYAN COLOXIES FROM ATLANTIS.
nodes.summary: Argues that the Aryans did not originate in central Asia. If they had, their branches would appear in Siberia, China, Japan and across Asia, and Europe would be filled with them as eastern Asia is with Turanian peoples. Instead, Aryans entered India from the Punjab, and their traditions say they came from the west, from Europe and Atlantis. Europe was already inhabited in the Stone and Bronze Ages, with Celts in Western Europe by 5000 B.C.

Argues Aryan/Japhetic peoples originated in Atlantis, citing Genesis, Winchell, Rawlinson, Max Müller, Armenia/Ararat, Iberian and Celtic links, and Plato. Donnelly's excerpts claim Atlantean inheritance of numerals, metals, religion, Vedic and Greek myths, and calendars. Rejects central Asian origin: Aryans entered India from the Punjab, traditions point west to Europe and Atlantis, and Europe was already settled by the Stone and Bronze Ages.

title: Atlantis Reconstructed: Ancient Dietary and Circumcision Customs as Evidence
key_items: Chapter XI.
A TLANTIS RECONSTR UCTED.
summary: The page argues that ancient practices suggest a wise, civilized Atlantean race. Egyptians, Ethiopians, and Israelites avoided pork, linked to trichina dangers and a Talmudic insect rule. Circumcision, practised by several ancient peoples, likely began in Atlantis, where a king Ouranos imposed it during a plague. Colonies spread the custom but not the disease, which reached Europe only after Columbus contacted the West Indies.

title: ATLANTIS BECONHTRVGTED.
summary: Describes the mythical island of Atlantis as the home of the antediluvians: a large volcanic island with smaller neighboring islands, a mild Azores-like climate, and four rivers flowing from a central point. Two races are covered, a dark, smaller-handed metalworking and navigating people and a tall, lighter-skinned people, with battles between them. It argues that shared customs across the Atlantic imply common origin, notes that domestic cattle and Old World cereals appear in Europe rather than America, and suggests Atlantean agriculture was advanced.

title: ATLANTIS RECOXSTIiUCTED.
summary: Describes Atlantean civilization: plough use, domesticated horses and livestock, crops, aqueducts, metalworking, and an alphabet. It covers their colonies spreading across the world, mixing with native peoples, and comparisons to Britain's colonial history. It also covers their monotheistic sun-centred religion, belief in immortality and embalming, and a kingly government with courts, monuments, trade, and advanced engineering. It ends by arguing Atlantis's loss would be unforgettable, urging underwater exploration, and noting that its artefacts could reshape understanding of human history.
